title: Capacity of the two-user Gaussian interference channel
formal:
Determine the weighted capacity function
\[F(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)=\sup_{(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(a,b,P_{1},P_{2})}\bigl(\lambda R_{1}+(1-\lambda)R_{2}\bigr)\]
for all \(a,b\in\mathbb R\), \(P_{1},P_{2}\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). The real memoryless channel is
\[Y_{1,t}=X_{1,t}+aX_{2,t}+Z_{1,t},\qquad Y_{2,t}=bX_{1,t}+X_{2,t}+Z_{2,t}.\]
The region \(C\) uses two independent private messages, deterministic separate encoders, average power over messages and time, no feedback or cooperation, and vanishing joint average decoding error, as defined below. The required absolute accuracy is \(1/100\) bit per real channel use everywhere on this domain.
definitions:
All five parameters are finite real numbers and remain fixed as block length grows. Negative, zero, and positive gains are included; powers may be zero or arbitrarily large. The two direct gains and the noise variances are normalized to one. For every \(i\in\{1,2\}\) and time \(t\), the noise \(Z_{i,t}\) has density \((2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-z^{2}/2)\) on \(\mathbb R\). All these noises are mutually independent and independent of both messages. There is no fading, channel state, or additional channel memory. Channel parameters and both codebooks are known to all terminals.

For a positive integer \(K\), let \([K]=\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\). An \((n,K_{1},K_{2})\) code has \(n,K_{1},K_{2}\ge1\), two independent uniform messages \(M_{i}\in[K_{i}]\), deterministic encoders \(f_{i}:[K_{i}]\to\mathbb R^{n}\), and Borel-measurable decoders \(d_{i}:\mathbb R^{n}\to[K_{i}]\). Transmitter \(i\) sends \(X_{i}^{n}=f_{i}(M_{i})\), and receiver \(i\) estimates only its own message using \(d_{i}(Y_{i}^{n})\). Each code must satisfy
\[\frac{1}{nK_{i}}\sum_{m\in[K_{i}]}\sum_{t=1}^{n}f_{i}(m)_{t}^{2}\le P_{i},\qquad i=1,2.\]
This is a separate power budget for each transmitter, averaged over messages and time. It is not a bound on every symbol or every individual codeword, and power cannot be transferred between transmitters. The error is
\[P_{e}=\Pr\bigl[d_{1}(Y_{1}^{n})\ne M_{1}\ \text{or}\ d_{2}(Y_{2}^{n})\ne M_{2}\bigr],\]
averaged over the independent uniform messages and all Gaussian noise. There is no maximal-error-over-messages requirement. The encoders may depend arbitrarily on time and their own messages, with arbitrary real codeword entries and no computation bound. They have no shared random seed, common message, feedback, or communication link; neither encoder knows the other message. The receivers cannot communicate. Predetermined time sharing, unequal powers in different phases, and arbitrary temporal dependence within each codeword are allowed subject to the displayed average budgets. There is no secrecy or prescribed signaling-distribution constraint.

All rate logarithms have base two. A nonnegative rate pair \((R_{1},R_{2})\) is achievable if there is a code for each integer block length \(n\ge1\), with message sizes \(K_{i,n}\), such that \(P_{e,n}\to0\) and
\[\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_{2}K_{i,n}}{n}\ge R_{i},\qquad i=1,2.\]
The region \(C(a,b,P_{1},P_{2})\) is the Euclidean closure of all achievable pairs. It is a nonempty compact convex downward-closed subset of \([0,c_{1}]\times[0,c_{2}]\), where \(c_{i}=\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{i})\); hence \(F\) is finite. These are bits per one real scalar channel use, not per complex channel use. No finite block code must attain a boundary rate. The weights include both endpoints, and the exact supporting function determines the closed region. The task has real mathematical parameters; it does not silently restrict them or the codebooks to rational encodings.
answer_criterion:
Supply one unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on \(\mathbb R^{2}\times\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{2}\times[0,1]\) and a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that, for every tuple in this domain,
\[|g(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)-F(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The proof must justify both sides of this error against the operational code definition, using its average-power and average-error conventions and bits per real use. Certified lower and upper bounds of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by their midpoint. An exact function also qualifies. A formula or another unambiguous mathematical description may be used; no single-letter syntax, fixed number of auxiliary variables, polynomial evaluation bound, or finite encoding of arbitrary real inputs is required. Any proposed evaluation rule must have a proved meaning and the stated guarantee on the full real domain. An unevaluated restatement of the capacity optimization or its limiting code definition, a sampled plot, and bounds with an unclosed gap do not determine the answer. Sum capacity alone, a restricted signaling optimum, a special interference regime, or an asymptotic high-power approximation is insufficient. The fixed tolerance does not assert an exact capacity theorem.
why: A defining problem in network information theory: even two interfering sender–receiver pairs expose limits of our ability to characterize optimal communication. An exact solution would distinguish which forms of message splitting, interference decoding and power allocation are fundamentally necessary.

importance.reason: A foundational multi-user capacity frontier with a simple channel model, strong approximate results and unresolved exact tradeoffs. Recent disputed claims make the precise formulation and status record especially valuable.

progress.text: Strong-interference capacity and the Han–Kobayashi achievable region establish fundamental benchmarks; later exact sum-rate results cover additional regimes without giving every rate tradeoff.
The checked v2 of Etkin–Tse–Wang states and proves the universal one-bit approximation in its complex-channel formulation; the journal version appeared in 2008.
Huleihel–Merhav withdraw the preprint originally used in this card’s provenance, acknowledging that Gaussian memory does not improve the power-controlled comparison region.
Nair–Ng’s published temporal-correlation invariance theorem concerns the Gaussian Han–Kobayashi region with time sharing.
Nair–Zhao establish a parameter condition removing multiplexing from an optimized Gaussian Z-channel inner region.
Nair–Zhao give restricted Gaussian-suboptimality examples without power control and retain the full power-controlled Gaussian-capacity conjecture.
Gohari–Nair–Zhao present an auxiliary-receiver outer bound; its full Gaussian specialization gives the stated very-weak-interference and one-sided conclusions.
Khandani v12 claims weak-interference capacity optimality of Gaussian Han–Kobayashi signaling. The complete proof has not been independently validated in this review.

status_note: Individually checked on 14 September 2026; retained as uncertain. Khandani 2501.14941v12, dated 7 September 2026, claims Gaussian Han–Kobayashi optimality for weak interference. The current primary PDF’s statement and §§7–8 were read, but its full proof for unrestricted codes was not independently validated; the scope is not an all-real-parameter capacity function. Nair–Zhao’s January manuscript questions parts of an earlier version and proves only a restricted single-phase Gaussian-suboptimality result without power control, not a refutation of v12 or of the full power-controlled region. Other checked 2025–2026 work supplies special inner-region and outer-bound results. The original Huleihel–Merhav reference was withdrawn in April 2018. Bounded later-work checks found no verified full answer at this card’s 1/100 tolerance; dated discussion of exact capacity alone is not a certification that this numerical benchmark is unsolved.

context_blocks.text: Two separately informed transmitters use the same medium, so each receiver observes its desired signal plus interference and Gaussian noise. The point-to-point rate \(c_{i}=\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{i})\) is an individual upper bound, but the two upper bounds generally cannot be reached together. The target describes every tradeoff between the independent conversations; knowing only their best total rate leaves other supporting weights undetermined.

The general two-user model is a foundational network information theory problem. Han–Kobayashi regions are established achievable inner bounds, and several structured parameter regimes have exact capacity or exact sum-capacity results. Shang and Chen’s monograph explicitly distinguishes these two kinds of conclusions. An optimal value within one specified signaling family is also different from a converse bounding every permitted code.

For strong interference, \(|a|\ge1\) and \(|b|\ge1\), the known capacity region is given by \(0\le R_{i}\le c_{i}\) and
\[R_{1}+R_{2}\le\min\!\left\{\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{1}+a^{2}P_{2}),\ \tfrac12\log_{2}(1+b^{2}P_{1}+P_{2})\right\}.\]
These are the two Gaussian multiple-access sum bounds in this card’s real normalization. With \(a=b=0\), capacity is the rectangle \([0,c_{1}]\times[0,c_{2}]\). The solved cases explain why an answer must retain both gains and both powers, rather than assume symmetry or a single interference-strength ordering.

Etkin, Tse and Wang establish the celebrated universal one-bit approximation using achievable and outer regions. The checked preprint’s formal model is complex-valued, and its error notion is an additive coordinate gap, not a bound on the error of a plotted sum-rate curve. That constant-gap theorem is a major approximate characterization, but it is not a certificate at this card’s much smaller tolerance in bits per real use. Its units and power convention must be accounted for in any precise transfer to this model.

Nair and Ng prove that allowing temporally correlated vector Gaussian inputs in the multiletter Han–Kobayashi region gives the same region as scalar Gaussian inputs when the comparison includes time sharing and its power allocation. This is an invariance theorem within a signaling class. It does not rule out other input distributions or establish full capacity. Huleihel and Merhav’s older preprint claiming an improvement from Gaussian memory was withdrawn in April 2018; its original abstract must not be counted as a valid advance.

Nair and Zhao’s ISIT 2025 work settles a structural conjecture about the Gaussian-signaling region for the one-sided, or Z, channel. Under its explicit parameter condition, multiplexing is unnecessary for the optimum of that inner region. The theorem does not assert that the inner region equals capacity for all Z channels.

Their January 2026 manuscript gives parameters where non-Gaussian distributions outperform Gaussian ones in a restricted single-phase superposition region without power control. Its Conjecture 1 still concerns the full Gaussian Han–Kobayashi region including power allocation over time. Section II.D explains that the new counterexample regime is disjoint from the regime in which the previous no-multiplexing theorem applies. Thus these results do not jointly yield a counterexample to the full capacity conjecture. Remark 2 also records the authors’ inability to verify parts of an earlier Khandani proof claim.

Gohari, Nair and Zhao’s February 2026 manuscript combines converse bounds through auxiliary receivers. The full Gaussian discussion in Section II.C restricts its matching corner, sum-rate and slope conclusions to the stated very-weak-interference regime and corresponding one-sided specializations. These conclusions must not be expanded to arbitrary weak interference merely from the broader abstract wording. The paper supplies an outer bound, not the general capacity function.

Khandani’s current v12, posted on 7 September 2026, claims that Gaussian Han–Kobayashi signaling attains weak-interference capacity with at most two time-sharing phases. Its equations use nonnegative squared cross-gain parameters under square roots; those symbols are not this card’s possibly signed amplitude gains. Sections 7–8 present the claimed converse and optimality conclusion. This review checked that statement and scope but did not establish the correctness of the full proof for unrestricted codes. Nair–Zhao’s January criticism predates this revision and is not automatically a refutation of it. The claim covers a major subdomain and is recorded under uncertain status, without asserting a solution over all real gains.

The user explicitly restored this real-parameter supporting-function target on 12 September 2026. The present review retains its full domain, average-power convention, and absolute \(1/100\) numerical acceptance. It does not add a requirement for a particular finite-letter characterization, and it does not infer fixed-tolerance unsolvability from sources discussing exact capacity.

sentences: Two separately informed transmitters communicate through real Gaussian noise while interfering with each other’s receivers.
The target is the weighted support function of the capacity region for every real gain, nonnegative power budget and weight between zero and one.
The model permits deterministic time sharing and averages each transmitter’s power over messages and time, with vanishing joint average decoding error.
Known special cases and approximation results leave the general tradeoff unresolved in the checked sources, while a September 2026 weak-interference capacity claim remains unverified here.
A complete Lean proof must certify one function within absolute error 1/100 bit per real channel use throughout the entire domain.
